items.title: DADR
items.text:
Record human decisions in a simple file format. Implement the data analysis using any tools you like. Assess conformity of the code with decisions automatically.

DADR workflow: draft, review, accept or reject, then audit, report, or supersede Draft • Write a data analysis decisionfrom scratch• Ask an LLM to read an existingcode base and identify key decisions Review Only a human analyst is allowed toapprove or reject decision records Accept Reject Audit • Substantive review: humans must agreewith all decisions• Code review: AI ensures that the codefaithfully implements decisions Report • Methods section• Decision tables• Onboarding documents Supersede • Revert a past decision• Tweak a previous choice

items.title: Problem 1: Opacity
items.text:
Every data analysis rests on dozens of choices: which observations to include, how to code key variables, which model to fit, how to quantify uncertainty. These choices matter: Many Analysts studies show that independent teams given the same data and hypotheses routinely reach different results.1

Most of these choices never appear in a methods section, and reconstructing them from code and data after the fact is an archeology project.

A simple way to record what was decided, why, what alternatives were considered, and what the consequences are.

items.title: Problem 2: Drift
items.text:
On long projects, analysts lose track of key decisions and the reasons behind them. The code drifts from the original intent, and minor-looking choices can change how results are interpreted. The risk grows when analysis is delegated to coding agents, which produce a lot of hard-to-review code.

A human-approved, auditable, and authoritative record of the key decisions made in a project.

items.title: Solution: Data Analysis Decision Records
items.text:
Data Analysis Decision Records (DADR) are designed to make our key analytical choices explicit. Each decision becomes a short Markdown record, stored alongside the code, data, and prose of a project. The DADR markdown files are human-editable, LLM-readable, and version-controllable. They include meta-data fields and tags that enable external tools to track decision flows, audit the faithfulness of a codebase to recorded decisions, and generate reports and narratives directly from the decision ledger.

DADR is not meant to be a comprehensive record of every thought, but rather a focused ledger of the key decisions that shape an analysis. It is a simple specification inspired by the Architecture Decision Record, a proven and popular development practice in the software engineering community.

Every candidate decision must be approved by the human analyst before it enters the permanent record.

Reviewing a candidate in the DADRock web UI Inbox.

items.title: New possibilities
items.text: A complete, structured trace of analytic decisions is more than documentation. It is an asset that downstream tools and humans can act on.

items.title: Faithfulness
items.text: Compare code, plan, and manuscript against recorded decisions to flag drift, undocumented choices, or contradictions. An LLM walks the relevant code paths and produces a discrepancy report for human triage.

items.title: Compliance
items.text: Cross-check decisions against a Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP), a Pre-Analysis Plan (PAP), Pre-registration, or data cleaning plan to surface deviations and unexecuted commitments.

items.title: Multiverse and robustness
items.text: Automatically surface the choices that need to be subjected to sensitivity, robustness, or multiverse analysis.

items.title: Decision flow
items.text: Follow how analytic choices evolved: which decisions superseded which, when, and why.

items.title: Drafting
items.text: Generate methods sections, appendices, and decision tables directly from the trace, with citations back to the records.

items.title: Onboarding
items.text: Hand a collaborator or new contributor a readable narrative instead of a code-archaeology assignment.

items.title: Replication and reuse
items.text: Give independent analysts a self-contained rationale for every consequential choice.

items.title: Coverage and audit
items.text: Report which analysis activities are backed by decisions, which are unreviewed, and which have gone stale.

items.title: Teaching
items.text: Use real annotated analyses to show how defensible alternatives were considered and chosen.

items.title: Example
items.text:
---
title: Drop observations with missing treatment assignment
status: accepted
id: 01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333
tags:
  - kind/sample
  - confidence/high
---

## Context

The randomization log is missing the treatment field for 47 of 8,213
respondents. Without an assignment we cannot estimate either
intent-to-treat or per-protocol effects for those rows. This extends
the sampling rule established in [[01938b8e4d70]].

## Decision

> #axis/sample/complete-case
> Drop the 47 respondents without recorded treatment assignment from
> the analysis sample.

## Alternatives

- Multiple imputation of the assignment indicator (rejected: assignment
  is a treatment, not a covariate; imputing it would invent
  counterfactual exposures).
- Coding the missing rows as control (rejected: silently biases the ITT
  estimate toward the null).

## Consequences

The analysis sample drops from 8,213 to 8,166. Power calculations need
to be re-run; see [[01938c30b1e2]].
Documentation Software

  1. Many Analysts studies:

    • Silberzahn et al. (2018), "Many Analysts, One Data Set: Making Transparent How Variations in Analytic Choices Affect Results," Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 1(3): 337–356, doi:10.1177/2515245917747646.
    • Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), "Variability in the Analysis of a Single Neuroimaging Dataset by Many Teams," Nature 582: 84–88, doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9.
    • Huntington-Klein et al. (2021), "The Influence of Hidden Researcher Decisions in Applied Microeconomics," Economic Inquiry 59(3): 944–960, doi:10.1111/ecin.12992.
    • Breznau et al. (2022), "Observing Many Researchers Using the Same Data and Hypothesis Reveals a Hidden Universe of Uncertainty," PNAS 119(44): e2203150119, doi:10.1073/pnas.2203150119.

    ↩

items.title: Changing decisions
items.text:
Once approved, a decision's substantive content is preserved. Corrections that leave the meaning intact, such as fixed spelling, formatting, links, or citations, are made in the record itself. Changing the decision, however slightly, means accepting a successor that supersedes the original.

The original remains accepted, and its successors field names the records that supersede it. “Superseded” describes an accepted record with successors, not a fourth stored status. DADRock keeps superseded records in its archive, next to rejected ones, and offers a superseded filter for convenience. The web interface's Ledger lists the decisions in force; Show archived adds the rejected and superseded records.

items.title: Correcting a record
items.text:
To correct a decided record, edit it. In the web interface or the standalone app, Edit opens the record's Markdown in place, on every record; on a decided record, a note above the editor says the edit is for corrections. You can also open the file in your usual editor. The record keeps its ID and stays in its folder. When you save from the web interface, DADRock refuses to change the id, status, or successors of an accepted, superseded, or rejected record, and an accepted record must keep its four required sections, each once and with text; the title, body, tags, and front-matter keys outside DADR can change.

Whether an edit corrects a record or changes the decision is a judgment no rule can make (specification §6.3), so DADRock makes every edit visible instead of forbidding it. The record's history lists the edits Git recorded to its title and body since it was accepted or rejected, including changes not committed yet, and dadrock validate changes reports them with their diffs.

Agents never edit decided text. The edit-record agent task revises candidates only; for a decision in force, Revise with agent and Fix with agent draft a successor instead, and archived records offer no agent fix.

items.title: Drafting a successor
items.text:
To change what was decided, draft a successor: a new candidate that supersedes the old record, its predecessor. The predecessor stays in force until you accept the successor.

  • Supersede on a record in the Ledger opens a full-page successor draft on the Draft page. It starts from the record's exact title, tags, and body and asks "Why does this decision change?"; the reason is optional. Add a decision to merge attaches more decisions in force to supersede them together with one successor (a merge); the draft then starts untitled, from every predecessor's sections and tags. Create candidate saves the successor candidate and opens it in the Inbox. Supersede with existing decisions instead links an accepted record to successors that already exist.
  • Revise with agent on the record opens the Draft page, which asks "What changed, and why?" and sends your answer to the supersede-record task; the task asks a local agent to draft the successor. The task takes one or more accepted records and the change you want. The agent starts from the predecessor's exact text and changes only what the request requires, so the successor reads as a small diff; for several predecessors it combines them into one decision. It returns the reason separately, and DADRock writes it into ## Supersedes when you save the proposal as a candidate.
  • You can also write the candidate yourself.

The successor names its predecessors in a ## Supersedes section, optionally followed by the reason for the change:

## Supersedes

[[01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333|Winsorize income at p99]]

Winsorizing at p99 still left implausible incomes in two waves.

The section starts with one or more lines, each exactly one record link by full UUID, [[uuid]] or [[uuid|label]]. The text after the links, if any, is the reason, in ordinary Markdown. A record has at most one ## Supersedes section, and the section must start with a link; acceptance refuses a candidate that breaks either rule, although dadrock validate does not report it. When DADRock writes the section, from the web interface, a supersede-record result, or MCP, it is the first section of the body, each link is labeled with the predecessor's title, and the reason follows the links.

items.title: Accepting a successor
items.text:
In the Inbox, a successor candidate opens on a Changes tab: the reason from its ## Supersedes section, then the difference from its predecessor, with a changed title, the tags added and removed, and a line diff of the body without ## Supersedes. The Document tab shows the record itself. A successor of several decisions opens on a section view, Decision first, with each predecessor's text followed by the new text; Compare with switches to a line diff against one predecessor.

Accepting a successor adds its id to each predecessor's successors and moves each predecessor to dadr/archive/ with its body unchanged. The ## Supersedes section stays in the successor's body as the record of why the decision changed. It is a DADRock convention, not an additional required section of the DADR format. A superseded record says where the decision went ("Superseded by …", linking the decisions now in force); it keeps Edit but has no Supersede or Revise with agent.

  • One-to-one: the successor names one predecessor.
  • Merge: one successor names several predecessors, and each gains the successor's id.
  • Split: several successors name the same predecessor. Accept them together so that the predecessor gains all of their ids at once.

The Inbox shows candidates that supersede the same decision as one item, "Split “X” into 2 decisions", with each candidate's reason and diff. Select the ones that belong together and choose Accept selected: all of them to split the decision, or one of them to choose between competing alternatives. Reject the others one by one. From a terminal, accept them together with --with:

dadrock accept "Impute income" --with "Complete cases for the outcome"

--with repeats, and the positional words still join into one query. In general, accepting a set of candidates adds, for each predecessor named in the set, every candidate in the set that names it. Candidates without ## Supersedes are simply accepted.

DADRock checks the whole set before writing anything: every candidate must meet the acceptance requirements, and every named predecessor must exist, be accepted, not already be superseded, and not be in the set. A predecessor that is already superseded is refused with the names of its current successors. If a write fails partway, every record is restored.

For two records that are already accepted, dadrock supersede --from OLD --to NEW links them explicitly and moves OLD to dadr/archive/. Records linked this way have no ## Supersedes section, so no reason is recorded.

items.title: Stale successors
items.text:
Two candidates that name the same predecessor may be the halves of a split or competing alternatives; you decide by what you accept together. Once one of them is accepted alone, the other is stale: its predecessor was superseded after it was drafted, like a branch whose base has moved. dadrock validate warns about a stale candidate (stale_supersedes) and names the decisions now in force, and acceptance refuses it. Point its ## Supersedes link at the current decision, or reject it.

DADRock never retargets a link on its own. In the Inbox, a stale successor shows a warning that names the decisions now in force, and Accept waits until you choose Retarget, which points the link in ## Supersedes at the current decision (you pick one when there are several), saves the candidate, and shows the diff against it.

Validation also warns when an accepted record's ## Supersedes section names a predecessor that does not list it in successors (unlinked_supersedes), for example after a record was accepted by hand.

items.title: History
items.text:
A decision's history is its chain of versions, linked by supersession, plus the corrections made to each version. DADRock derives the versions from successors alone, so they need no extra front matter and no Git. Corrections stay in the record itself, and DADRock reads them from Git.

In the web interface, a record's History tab shows the decision's versions newest first, the opened one highlighted and the current ones labeled. Lanes join where a decision was split and fork where several were merged. Each change shows its reason and, on request, its diff. Records at the other end of a split or merge appear on one line ("Also became …", "Merged with …") and link to the record. Under each version, "Edited 2 times since accepted" lists its text edits newest first: the date, the author, and the commit subject, each with its diff. An edit that is not committed yet comes first, marked "Not committed yet". A record whose text changed after acceptance shows "Edited since acceptance" ("Edited since rejection" for a rejected record) next to its file name, which opens the History tab. Outside a Git repository, History shows the versions without edits.

From a terminal:

dadrock history QUERY            # versions as a graph, newest first
dadrock history QUERY --patch    # with the diff of each change and each text edit
dadrock history QUERY --json
dadrock diff OLD NEW             # compare any two records

QUERY is any version: a full id, an id prefix, a filename, or a title. The history of a record contains:

  • versions: the record, its predecessors back to the first version, and its successors forward to the current ones;
  • current versions: the versions without successors;
  • links: each supersession between two records, with its reason, the text after the links in the successor's ## Supersedes section. Records linked with dadrock supersede alone have no reason;
  • neighbors: records at the other end of a link that are not versions, listed on one line without their own history;
  • text edits: for each version, the edits Git recorded to its title or body since the version was accepted or rejected, newest first.

Versions are listed newest first, and a record always appears above its predecessors, even when it was created earlier. ◉ marks the record you asked for. A decision superseded by several records is a split; several decisions superseded by one record are a merge:

●   0193b2a1d117  Multiple imputation for income  current
│ ● 0193b2a1c0f4  Complete cases for the outcome  current
├─╯ Outcome and covariates need different treatment.
●   01938c20a3b4  Listwise deletion
│   Complete cases lose a third of the sample.
◉   01938a77e310  Pairwise deletion

◉   0193c4e1a2b0  One outlier rule for all covariates  current
├─╮ The two rules disagreed at the 99th percentile.
● │ 0193a0b7e911  Winsorize income at p99
│ ● 01939f2c4d07  Drop implausible ages
●   01938f11aa02  Trim income at p95

The history from one half of a split shows the other half as a neighbor ("also became …"), and the history from one input of a merge shows the other input as a neighbor ("merged with …").

Diffs compare the title, the tags, and the body without ## Supersedes, after normalizing line endings; other front matter is not compared. --patch prints each link's diff under it: the title change, the tag changes (+topic/missing-data −topic/attrition), and the changed lines with a few lines of context. dadrock diff OLD NEW prints the same comparison for any two records, linked or not. Diffs are computed when shown and never stored.

The history ignores successor ids that match no record and stops at cycles, with a warning; dadrock validate reports both. The local web server serves the same JSON at /api/records/{id}/history (?patch=1 for diffs) and /api/records/{id}/diff?against={other}, which compares {other} to {id}.

items.title: Text edits
items.text:
A correction that leaves the meaning intact, such as a fixed typo, link, or citation, is made in the record itself and keeps its id (specification §6.3). DADRock never copies these edits into records. It reads them from Git with git log --follow on the version's file, which follows the moves between inbox/, ledger/, and archive/:

  • The baseline is the earliest commit in which the record is accepted or rejected. Edits made while it was a candidate are not listed.
  • Every later commit whose title or body (without ## Supersedes, line endings aside) differs from the previous commit's is an edit. A commit that changes only tags, successors, or the folder is not.
  • A change not committed yet, the working tree against HEAD, is listed first.

A version with edits gets one line under it in the graph, and --patch adds each edit's diff under a header with the commit's short hash and subject:

◉   01938c20a3b4  Winsorize income at p99  current
    edited 2 times since accepted (latest 2026-10-01, Alice)

In JSON, each version has edits, newest first. Each edit is {commit, short_commit, author, date, subject, title_changed, body_changed}, plus diff with --patch; date is the author date in ISO 8601, and the commit fields are null for an edit not committed yet. Candidates have no edits ([]). Outside a Git repository, or without git, edits is null and the rest of the history is unchanged.

Listing the edits does not judge them. Whether an edit is a correction or a change of decision is the reviewer's call; to change the decision, supersede the record instead.

items.title: Checking changes
items.text:
Once a record is accepted or rejected, its id and status do not change, and entries are not removed from its successors. Its title and body take corrections that leave the meaning intact; changing the decision means superseding the record (specification §6.3). dadrock validate changes checks the first rule against Git and shows every title and body edit, so a reviewer can judge the second:

dadrock validate changes                      # working tree against HEAD
dadrock validate changes --staged             # staged changes against HEAD
dadrock validate changes --base origin/main   # everything since another revision
dadrock validate changes --strict             # title and body edits are errors too

For each record file in dadr/inbox/, dadr/ledger/, or dadr/archive/ that changed since the base revision, DADRock reads the file's version at the base. If that version was accepted or rejected, DADRock compares the current version with it. A record that moved between folders, by being accepted, rejected, or superseded, is followed through Git's rename detection or by its id.

  • Errors: a changed id (record_id_changed) or status (record_status_changed), a removed successors entry (successor_removed), or a file that no longer parses (invalid_record). The message names the record; for a changed id or status, it suggests drafting a successor instead, or a new candidate for a rejected record.
  • Warnings, with the diff: an edited title (record_title_edited) or body (record_body_edited; line endings aside). The message names the record and says what to do instead if the edit changes the decision: supersede it, or draft a new candidate for a rejected record. The text output prints the diff under the warning: the old and new title, or the changed body lines with a few lines of context. In JSON, the issue's diff carries the same change: title with old and new, or the body's lines, each {kind, text} with kind one of context, added, or removed.
  • Deleting an accepted or rejected record is a warning (record_deleted).
dadrock validate changes: 0 error(s), 1 warning(s) (working tree against HEAD (5309d425ba44))
[warning] record_body_edited /home/me/analysis/dadr/ledger/winsorize-income-at-p99.md: the body of accepted record `Winsorize income at p99` (01938c20a3b4) was edited since HEAD. If this changes the decision, supersede the record instead.

      ## Consequences

    - Estimates are less sensitive to outliers.
    + Estimates are much less sensitive to outliers.

tags, keys outside DADR, and new successors entries change freely, and so do candidates. New files have no earlier version to compare, and a repository without commits passes. Warnings alone exit with status zero. With --strict, title and body edits are errors too, for projects that want accepted text frozen; there is no project setting, so pass the flag wherever the check runs. Outside a Git repository, or when the base revision does not resolve, the command fails. Ordinary dadrock validate does not use Git.

items.title: In continuous integration
items.text:
To review what a pull request changes in accepted and rejected records, compare it with its target branch. The checkout needs that branch's history:

git fetch origin main
dadrock validate
dadrock validate changes --base origin/main

A changed id or status, or a removed successor, fails the check. Title and body edits appear in the CI log as warnings with their diffs, so a reviewer can tell a correction from a change of decision. A project that wants accepted text frozen adds --strict, which fails the check on those edits too:

dadrock validate changes --base origin/main --strict

--base origin/main compares with the tip of main. That is right when the checkout already includes main, such as the merge commit many CI services check out for a pull request. For a branch that main has moved past, compare with the point where the branch started: --base "$(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)". A CLI-only CI build can use the no-js-build feature.

items.title: In a pre-commit hook
items.text:
To catch changes before they are committed, run the check on the staged changes in a pre-commit hook, .git/hooks/pre-commit, made executable:

#!/bin/sh
exec dadrock validate changes --staged

The hook blocks a commit only on errors; title and body edits print as warnings. Add --strict to block those edits too. Git runs hooks from the repository root. If the project lives in a subdirectory, such as analysis/dadr/, change into that subdirectory first: cd analysis && exec dadrock validate changes --staged.

items.title: Making decisions
items.text: A Data Analysis Decision Record answers one question: what did we decide, and why? Keep one Markdown file per consequential choice, alongside your analysis.

items.title: Four sections
items.text:
• Context: the question and relevant evidence.
  • Decision: what you chose, stated directly.
  • Alternatives: other approaches considered and why you set them aside.
  • Consequences: implications, tradeoffs, and follow-up work.

A file also has three required YAML fields: title, status, and id. DADRock generates the ID for you. Tags and links are optional; you do not need a classification system to get started.

items.title: Example
items.text:
---
title: Drop observations with missing treatment assignment
status: accepted
id: 01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333
tags:
  - kind/sample
  - confidence/high
---

## Context

The randomization log is missing the treatment field for 47 of 8,213
respondents. Without an assignment we cannot estimate either

the sampling rule established in [[01938b8e4d70]].

## Decision

> Drop the 47 respondents without recorded treatment assignment from
> the analysis sample.

## Alternatives

- Multiple imputation of the assignment indicator (rejected: assignment
  is a treatment, not a covariate; imputing it would invent
  counterfactual exposures).
- Coding the missing rows as control (rejected: silently biases the ITT

## Consequences

The analysis sample drops from 8,213 to 8,166. Power calculations need

items.title: Draft, review, preserve
items.text:
A new record is a candidate. A human reviews it and marks it accepted or rejected. Acceptance keeps the same ID. An agent may help draft a candidate, but cannot decide whether you endorse it.

Once approved, a decision's substantive content is preserved. Corrections that leave the meaning intact are made in place; changing the decision means accepting a successor that supersedes it. See Changing decisions.

items.title: What deserves a record?
items.text:
Start with choices a collaborator would ask you to explain: who enters the sample, how a variable is defined, why a model was chosen, or how missing values are handled. Skip routine formatting and mechanical refactoring. A few useful explanations are better than an unmanageable review queue.

Code can reveal what an analysis does without revealing why. When a draft says the rationale is unknown, supply it or leave the record as a candidate until you can review it.

Install DADRock and open the web interface or the standalone app, or consult the full specification for exact syntax and implementation rules.

items.title: Project layout
items.text:
The DADR format does not mandate a directory structure. DADRock uses this one, created by dadrock init:

dadr/
  inbox/
    country-exclusions.md
  ledger/
    income-preprocessing.md
    drop-missing-treatment.md
  archive/
    deprecated-cohort-filter.md
  templates/
    candidate.md                # optional
  tasks/
  runs/
    .gitignore
Directory Contents dadr/inbox/ Candidates: proposals awaiting review dadr/ledger/ Decisions in force: accepted records without successors dadr/archive/ Records kept but no longer in force: rejected records and superseded records dadr/templates/ Optional template overrides for new candidates dadr/tasks/ Optional project-specific agent workflows and overrides of built-in tasks (dadr/tasks/<task-id>.md: YAML front matter for the manifest, Markdown body for the prompt) dadr/runs/ Agent-run inputs, results, and logs; ignored by version control

dadrock accept changes a candidate's status to accepted and moves the file from dadr/inbox/ to dadr/ledger/. dadrock reject changes it to rejected and moves it to dadr/archive/. The id never changes. Superseding a decision, by accepting its successor or with dadrock supersede, appends the successor's id to the predecessor's successors and moves the predecessor to dadr/archive/; its status stays accepted.

Filenames carry no meaning: DADRock identifies a record by its id, never by its filename (specification §5). It names a new record after its title, income-preprocessing.md, and adds the short id, income-preprocessing-01938b8e4d70.md, only when the inbox already has that name. Accepting, rejecting, and superseding keep the filename and change only the folder; the short id is added only when the target folder already has that name. A name that another record leaves in the same operation counts as free, so a successor with its predecessor's title takes the predecessor's filename in the ledger. Renaming a record file does not change the record.

The directory is a convenience: the front matter is authoritative. dadrock validate warns when a record sits in a directory that does not match its status and successors. Moving a file breaks relative Markdown links to its path; record wikilinks use ids and are unaffected. Use dadrock config to inspect the resolved layout. Keep the record directories in version control; run state may contain pasted context and source excerpts and is ignored by default. Clear agent runs, in the project menu of the web interface, deletes dadr/runs/.

Earlier versions of DADRock used candidates/, accepted/, and rejected/. DADRock no longer reads those directories: move candidates to inbox/, current decisions to ledger/, and rejected and superseded records to archive/.

items.title: LLM agents
items.text:
Agent assistance is optional: you can record decisions with DADRock alone. Agents can work with DADRock in three ways:

  • MCP: an agent client calls DADRock's tools through its Model Context Protocol server.
  • ACP: DADRock directs a local agent through the Agent Client Protocol to draft and revise candidates.
  • CLI: an agent that runs shell commands uses dadrock directly.

Whichever route you use, agent outputs are proposals for review. Code can show what happened without establishing why; correct unsupported claims and supply missing rationale before accepting. Acceptance and rejection remain human decisions.

items.title: MCP
items.text:
DADRock exposes a Model Context Protocol server over stdio:

dadrock mcp serve
dadrock mcp serve --read-only
dadrock mcp serve path/to/project

The normal server exposes inspection and mutation tools through the same command layer as the CLI: listing, searching, and reading records, lifecycle status, decision history and diffs, tags, tasks and task runs, validation, and a project snapshot; plus creating candidates, including successors that supersede decisions in force, and submitting task results. Use read-only mode for clients that should only inspect records. Lifecycle actions are not exposed over MCP: humans accept, reject, and supersede records in the web interface (also available in an editor panel) or with the CLI.

Register the server with your client as a stdio command. The configuration file and its location depend on the client; many accept an entry like this:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "dadrock": {
      "command": "dadrock",
      "args": ["mcp", "serve", "--read-only", "/path/to/project"]
    }
  }
}

items.title: ACP
items.text:
DADRock connects to a locally installed agent through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). The agent may use a remote model. You need an ACP-compatible provider or bridge and its authentication. An ordinary claude or codex executable alone is not necessarily an ACP provider.

Use your provider's own installation and authentication instructions. Choose a bridge explicitly supported by your agent provider. DADRock does not install providers or manage their credentials.

items.title: Configure one local agent
items.text:
DADRock looks for known provider commands on PATH, such as claude-agent-acp, codex-acp, or gemini --acp. To choose one, set DADROCK_ACP_AGENT to the executable and put any arguments in DADROCK_ACP_AGENT_ARGS, or pass --agent and --agent-arg to a single command. Check the connection:

dadrock agent check
dadrock agent skills

Every task carries its own instructions; no separately installed skill is required. agent skills lists optional local instructions, which dadrock agent draft --skill NAME can add to a draft.

DADRock attaches its own MCP server to its agent sessions by default. --no-mcp disables that attachment for providers where it is unsuitable.

items.title: Draft for review
items.text:
dadrock task run code-to-record --path analysis/ --limit 5
dadrock task run context-to-record --context "Explain our choice of sample restrictions"

The limit asks the agent to prioritize a small batch, rather than treating every operation as a decision. It is a drafting request, not a hard guarantee on model output. The web interface offers the same drafting actions, and the results of task runs, including those started from the command line, land in its Inbox.

On the command line, tool permission requests default to deny. When your selected workflow needs tools, explicitly choose the appropriate permission mode with --permission allow-once or --permission allow-always. Task runs started from the web interface allow each request once. This does not authorize an agent to accept decisions on your behalf.

dadrock agent draft remains available for compatibility. New workflows should use task run context-to-record.

items.title: Custom workflows and runs
items.text:
dadrock task list
dadrock task show code-to-record
dadrock task runs
dadrock task result RUN_ID

Built-in workflows include drafting, editing candidates, drafting successors for accepted decisions, merging drafts, finding conflicts, and synthesizing accepted decisions into a spec. The built-in tasks are the task guides of the dadr skill, the files in skills/dadr/tasks/ of this repository. Each is one Markdown file: its YAML front matter is the task manifest (id, inputs, requirements, and output kind) and its body is the prompt. Every task run gets read-only access to the MCP server plus task-result submission. dadrock task show <task-id> prints a task's prompt, and --json adds its manifest.

To customize a task, copy its guide with dadrock task show <task-id> --raw > dadr/tasks/<task-id>.md and adapt it. A project task overrides a user task in ~/.dadrock/tasks/<task-id>.md (or $DADROCK_TASKS_DIR), which overrides the built-in task with the same id. The file name must match the id in the front matter; dadrock task list reports files that do not load, including task directories in the old task.toml layout. Friendly input flags cover code-to-record (--path, --focus, --limit), context-to-record (--context), and decisions-to-spec (--focus). Other tasks, including your own, take their inputs, such as record_id or record_ids, as JSON with --input-json; do not combine it with the friendly flags.

Runs are persisted under dadr/runs/, which is ignored by default and may contain source excerpts or model transcripts. Output kinds determine how results are rendered. Protocol and run metadata stay outside record front matter.

items.title: CLI
items.text:
Coding agents that run shell commands can drive dadrock like any other tool. Its machine-readable output is a JSON command envelope with command, ok, and data, plus diagnostics and changed_paths when there are any. Commands such as list and new always print it; commands with a human-readable summary, such as validate, print it with --json:

dadrock commands --json
dadrock list --status candidate
dadrock new "Decision title"
dadrock validate --json

dadrock commands --json describes every command: its usage, whether it changes the project, whether it supports JSON, and when it exits non-zero. dadrock help COMMAND prints the same detail for one command. The full list is in the command-line reference.

For guidance beyond the built-in tasks, copy skills/dadr/ from this checkout to your agent's supported skill directory, such as .agents/skills/dadr or ~/.codex/skills/dadr. The agent's own discovery rules determine which location works. The skill routes requests such as bootstrapping candidates from existing code, finding conflicting decisions, or synthesizing a spec to its task guides, the same guides the built-in tasks run, and says how to deliver the results with dadrock commands.

Future automated faithfulness and coverage checks are described on the roadmap.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
These are proposed directions, not currently available guarantees or delivery commitments. See DADRock for current capabilities.

  • Change detection: inspect Git diffs of analysis code and suggest consequential choices worth documenting. Checking edits to accepted records against Git is already available (Checking changes).
  • Code-comment scanning: resolve #dadr/ annotations in analysis source files.
  • Faithfulness checks: compare accepted decisions with code, analysis plans, and manuscripts; report discrepancies for human review.
  • Reporting: draft methods sections and decision narratives with references to records. A built-in agent task already synthesizes accepted decisions into a spec (Custom workflows and runs).
  • Coverage and robustness: identify undocumented choices and possible sensitivity analyses.
  • Process metrics: compute review latency, coverage, and follow-through from appropriate lifecycle data.
  • Additional validation: citation resolution, plan-deviation requirements, and placeholder detection.

Future checks should help people investigate discrepancies. A missing link does not establish that an analysis is wrong, and a clean validation report does not establish scientific correctness.

items.title: DADR specification
items.text:
For a short introduction, see Making decisions. Suggested tag vocabularies are documented separately.

DADR (Data-Analysis Decision Records) is a file-first format for recording consequential decisions in empirical and data-analysis projects. A DADR record is a Markdown file that captures one analytic decision: the context that motivated it, the decision that was made, the alternatives considered, and the consequences for the analysis. Records live alongside the analysis code, manuscript, data references, and project documentation.

This page is the canonical specification of the record format. Directory layouts, inference, version-control hooks, previews, and agent workflows are tooling concerns; the reference implementation documents its own choices on the Project layout and Changing decisions pages and in the DADRock section.

items.title: Version
items.text:
This document defines DADR specification version 0.1.0-alpha.3.

DADR uses Semantic Versioning. Versions below 1.0.0 are alpha-stage specifications: breaking changes MAY appear in minor or patch releases while the model is still being validated. Starting with 1.0.0, breaking changes MUST increment the major version.

items.title: 1. Conventions
items.text:
The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, and MAY are normative when written in uppercase. Examples are non-normative.

Record — one Markdown file with DADR front matter and a body.

Record set — the records a tool is pointed at, such as all records in a project. Every rule that relates records to one another (unique identifiers, resolving links, supersession) is evaluated over the record set. This specification does not mandate where record files live.

items.title: 2. Records
items.text:
A record MUST describe exactly one decision or one proposed decision. Closely related choices SHOULD be split into separate records when they could be accepted, rejected, or superseded independently.

A record MUST be a single UTF-8 Markdown file without a byte-order mark. It consists of YAML front matter followed by a Markdown body.

The Markdown file is the source of truth. Indexes, databases, graphs, reports, and static sites built from records are derived and not canonical. Records MUST remain readable and editable with an ordinary text editor; tools are a convenience, not a requirement.

items.title: 3. Front matter
items.text:
A record MUST begin with YAML front matter delimited by --- lines. The front matter MUST be a YAML mapping with these keys:

Key Required Value title yes A non-empty, single-line string: a short noun phrase. 120 characters or fewer is recommended. status yes candidate, accepted, or rejected. See Lifecycle. id yes A UUIDv7 in lowercase hyphenated form. See Identifiers. successors no An array of ids of the accepted records that supersede this one. See Supersession. tags no An array of tags, written without the leading #. See Tags.

An omitted array and an empty array ([]) are equivalent.

Front matter MUST NOT record dates or times. A record's time is always derived from its id (Identifiers). In particular, front matter MUST NOT contain a date key, nor, under any key, a value written as an ISO 8601 date or date-time, such as 2026-05-07 or 2026-05-07T14:30:00Z.

Other keys MAY appear, for example author, aliases, or Pandoc's bibliography. They carry no DADR meaning. Tools MUST NOT reject a record because of them unless they break the date rule above, and tools that rewrite front matter MUST preserve them.

DADR expresses classifications such as kind, confidence, provenance, topic, or the people involved as tags rather than as dedicated keys. The Tags page suggests a vocabulary.

---
title: Drop observations with missing treatment assignment
status: candidate
id: 01938b8f-9d71-7456-8000-fedcba987654
tags:
  - kind/sample
  - writer/agent
---

items.title: 4. Body
items.text:
An accepted record MUST contain exactly one ## heading for each of the four standard sections. Headings match case-insensitively. A section's content runs from its heading to the next # or ## heading.

## Context

What problem, dataset, or constraint motivated this decision?

## Decision

What was decided? State the choice in one or two sentences, in the active voice.

## Alternatives

What other options were considered, and why were they set aside?

## Consequences

What follows for results, downstream analyses, robustness checks, or future work?

In an accepted record, each standard section MUST contain text other than whitespace and HTML comments. When nothing applies, say so in words; for example, "No alternatives were considered."

The sections MAY appear in any order. Records MAY add other sections, such as ## Robustness, ## Plan deviation, or ## Open questions. A candidate MAY omit or leave empty any section; the requirements above apply once it is accepted.

The four sections follow Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), a common software-engineering practice for capturing the context, choice, and consequences of a design decision in a short Markdown file. DADR applies the same structure to data analysis.

items.title: 5. Identifiers and filenames
items.text:
A record's id is a UUIDv7 (RFC 9562) written in lowercase canonical form (8-4-4-4-12, 36 characters). It is assigned when the record is created and never changes, including when the record is accepted or rejected. The id is the record's only stable key: titles, filenames, and locations may change.

UUIDv7 needs no shared counter, so concurrent branches and agents can create records safely. Its first 48 bits are a Unix-millisecond timestamp, so identifiers sort by creation time. That timestamp is the record's only date: records never store another one (§3). When a record was accepted, rejected, or superseded, and by whom, belongs to version control or tool logs, not to the record.

The short id is the first 12 hexadecimal digits of the id, with no hyphen:

id:        01938b8e-4d70-7abc-8def-0123456789ab
short id:  01938b8e4d70

Short ids MUST be unique within a record set. The short id encodes exactly the id's 48-bit timestamp, so two ids created in the same millisecond share it. Tools that create records MUST ensure uniqueness, for example by generating a fresh id in a later millisecond when the short id is already taken. The short id is the recommended form for displaying a record's identity and for linking to it.

Filenames are free. A short kebab-case slug of the title plus .md, such as income-preprocessing.md, is suggested. A filename carries no meaning: tools MUST NOT derive a record's identity or status from it, and a record keeps its id when it is renamed or moved.

Authors drafting by hand can take an id from the UUID v7 generator. A file without an id is not a valid record; tools MAY repair it by assigning a fresh id.

items.title: 6.1 Status
items.text:
Status Meaning candidate A proposed decision under review. accepted A human-approved decision, whether or not it has since been superseded. rejected A candidate closed without approval: rejected, withdrawn, duplicated, merged into another record, or no longer relevant.

The only transitions are candidate → accepted and candidate → rejected. Each changes the status of the same record and keeps its id. accepted and rejected are final. To revisit a rejected or superseded decision, create a new candidate.

A record's lifecycle stage is given by its status alone. Tools MUST NOT infer it from the file's name or location.

Acceptance is a human decision. Tools and agents MUST NOT accept a candidate without human approval, and a candidate MUST meet the body requirements to be accepted.

items.title: 6.2 Supersession
items.text:
To supersede an accepted decision, accept a new record and add its id to the old record's successors. An accepted record with a non-empty successors array is superseded. This is derived from the record set; it is not a status, and the old record's status stays accepted.

successors:
  - 01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333

Within a record set:

  • only accepted records MAY have a non-empty successors array;
  • each entry MUST be the id of an accepted record other than the record itself;
  • the graph formed by successors MUST be acyclic.

successors is an array, so one decision can be split into several successors, and several decisions can share one successor. Only the forward edge is stored; tools derive predecessors by scanning the record set. Supersession exists only in successors: a mention in prose or a wikilink does not supersede a record.

items.title: 6.3 Immutability
items.text:
Candidates MAY be edited freely. Once a record is accepted:

  • its id and status MUST NOT change, and entries MUST NOT be removed from successors;
  • the meaning of its title and body MUST NOT change. Corrections that leave the meaning intact, such as fixing spelling, formatting, links, or citations, are allowed.

tags and keys outside DADR MAY change. To change an accepted decision, create a new candidate, accept it, and supersede the old record.

The first rule can be checked mechanically, for example against version-control history. The second requires a reviewer's judgment. Tools can support that judgment by listing edits to accepted records, for example from version-control history.

items.title: 7. Tags
items.text:
DADR uses the Obsidian tag syntax:

  • in body text, a tag begins with #; in the front-matter tags array, it is written without #;
  • a tag consists of Unicode letters, numbers, emoji, _, -, and /, and contains no whitespace;
  • / separates levels of a hierarchy, so kind/sample is a child of kind; empty levels (a//b, a/, /a) are invalid;
  • a tag MUST contain at least one character other than a digit, _, -, or /, so #1984 is invalid and #y1984 is valid;
  • tags are case-insensitive: #Kind and #kind are the same tag.

DADR defines no required tag vocabulary. Projects choose their own; the Tags page suggests one.

Front-matter tags classify the whole record. Inline tags in the body attach to the passage they appear in; a common pattern is the first line of a blockquote. Tools SHOULD treat both as one tag set when indexing or reporting.

> #confidence/low
> The pre-analysis plan called for a complete-case rule. We now prefer multiple
> imputation, pending a check of missingness by site.

items.title: 7.1 Code tags
items.text:
In source-code comments, DADR tags carry a #dadr/ prefix that separates them from other comment text and other tag systems:

# #dadr/01938b8e4d70
df <- df[!is.na(df$treatment), ]

# #dadr/kind/measurement #dadr/topic/student-survey
survey["anx_mean"] = survey[["anx1", "anx2", "anx3"]].mean(axis=1)
  • #dadr/ followed by a short id or full id links the nearby code to that record. A link that does not resolve to a record in the record set is broken, and tools that check code tags SHOULD report it.
  • #dadr/ followed by any other tag annotates the nearby code with that tag; for example, #dadr/kind/measurement carries the tag kind/measurement.

Which lines of code a tag covers is defined by the tools that read it. Tags inside record files do not use the #dadr/ prefix.

items.title: 8.1 Links between records
items.text:
A wikilink whose target is a short id or a full id is a record link:

See [[01938c20a3b4]] for the sampling rule.
Compare with [[01938b8e4d70|the original preprocessing decision]].

The short id form is recommended. Hexadecimal digits match case-insensitively. A record link MUST resolve to a record in the record set, and tools MUST report links that do not resolve rather than guess a target. The form [[target|display text]] sets the displayed text.

Wikilinks with any other target are not DADR links, and tools MUST leave them unchanged. Tools MAY convert record links to ordinary Markdown links when rendering, for renderers that do not support wikilinks.

items.title: 8.2 Other links
items.text:
References to code, data, notebooks, manuscripts, plans, outputs, registries, and web pages SHOULD be standard Markdown links or autolinks, which every renderer supports. Relative paths resolve from the directory that contains the record, as in any Markdown renderer.

The exclusion is enforced in
[`analysis/build_sample.py` lines 42–58](../../analysis/build_sample.py#L42-L58),
following the pre-registration at <https://osf.io/abcde>.

items.title: 8.3 Citations
items.text: Records MAY cite sources with Pandoc citation syntax, such as [@rubin1976]. Resolving citation keys is up to the renderer. A Pandoc bibliography key in front matter is treated like any other key outside DADR.

items.title: 9. Conformance
items.text:
A record conforms if:

  1. it is a UTF-8 Markdown file without a byte-order mark, beginning with YAML front matter that is a mapping;
  2. title, status, and id are present and valid (§3, §5);
  3. the front matter contains no date key and no ISO 8601 date or date-time value (§3);
  4. successors, if present, is an array of UUIDv7 ids, and is empty unless status is accepted;
  5. tags, if present, is an array of valid tags (§7);
  6. if status is accepted, the body meets §4.

A record set conforms if every record in it conforms and:

  1. no two records share an id or a short id;
  2. every successors entry names another accepted record, and the successors graph is acyclic (§6.2);
  3. every record link resolves (§8.1).

A tool conforms if it:

  1. identifies records by id and lifecycle stage by status, never by filename or location;
  2. reports violations of these rules instead of silently guessing or repairing them;
  3. preserves front-matter keys it does not use when it rewrites a record;
  4. creates records with unique short ids;
  5. never accepts a candidate without human approval, and changes accepted records only as §6.3 allows.

A record's filename and location never affect whether it conforms (§5).

items.title: 10. Example record
items.text:
This example is non-normative.

---
title: Drop observations with missing treatment assignment
status: accepted
id: 01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333
tags:
  - kind/sample
---

# Drop observations with missing treatment assignment

## Context

The treatment variable is required for the primary estimand. Observations with
missing treatment assignment cannot contribute to the main comparison without
introducing an additional imputation model. See [[01938b8e4d70]] for how the
analysis sample was first defined.

## Decision

Drop observations with missing treatment assignment from the main analysis
sample.

## Alternatives

One alternative was to impute treatment assignment. This was not chosen because
the assignment mechanism is part of the study design rather than a downstream
measurement, and imputing it would make the estimand harder to interpret.

Another alternative was to keep the observations for descriptive tables only.
This can still be done in a supplemental descriptive analysis, but those rows
are excluded from the primary model.

## Consequences

The main sample size decreases. The manuscript should report the number of
excluded observations, and robustness checks should verify that treatment
missingness is not concentrated in one site.

items.title: Reference implementation
items.text: The reference implementation is DADRock, a Rust tool with a CLI, a web UI, and IDE integrations. See the Project layout page for the directories it uses, the DADRock command-line page for its commands and validation, and the Tags page for the recommended tag vocabulary.

items.title: Tags
items.text: You can use DADR without tags. Add them when they help your team find related decisions; there is no mandatory vocabulary.

items.title: Start small
items.text:
These are suggested conventions, not reserved fields or required categories:

Tag Meaning kind/sample Which observations enter the analysis kind/modeling Model specification and estimator kind/inference Uncertainty, tests, and intervals writer/agent An agent drafted the record confidence/low The choice is tentative or weakly supported people/decider/alice Person responsible for the choice axis/sample/complete-case A choice along a robustness or specification axis rejected/duplicate Why a candidate was closed

Use project-specific tags when they are useful. Existing vocabularies remain valid; there is no need to migrate records just to follow these examples.

items.title: Where to put them
items.text:
In YAML front matter, omit the leading #:

tags:
  - kind/sample
  - people/decider/alice

In prose, include it:

The exclusion rule is one sensitivity-analysis option. #axis/sample/complete-case

Use one spelling per concept and avoid near-duplicates. See the specification for exact syntax and normalization rules.

items.title: Recommended vocabulary
items.text: When a few tags are not enough, use this vocabulary. The DADR agent skill and DADRock's task prompts follow it. It is still a suggestion: DADRock does not enforce it, and a project's own conventions take precedence.

items.title: Kinds
items.text:
kind/ is the main classification: which part of the analysis a decision is about. Most records need one kind/ value: pick the closest match.

Tag Decisions about kind/setup The computing environment: software and package versions, random seeds, configuration kind/input Data sources: which datasets, versions, and extracts are used, and how they are obtained kind/sample Which units and observations enter the analysis: inclusion and exclusion rules, filters, joins, time windows kind/measurement How constructs become variables: outcome, treatment, and covariate definitions, coding, scales, derived scores kind/transformation How values are processed: cleaning, transforms, winsorizing, standardizing, imputation kind/exploration Exploratory analysis: descriptive checks and diagnostics that inform later choices kind/modeling Model specification: estimand, estimator, formula, fixed or random effects, priors kind/inference Uncertainty and testing: standard errors, intervals, tests, multiple-comparison adjustments kind/robustness Sensitivity analysis: alternative specifications, placebo and falsification checks kind/visualization Figures: plot types, encodings, scales kind/communication Reporting to readers: which results appear, tables, captions, labels, rounding, wording kind/output Produced artifacts: which result files and datasets are written, in what format, and where kind/governance Process: preregistration, plan deviations, ethics and data-access constraints, sign-off kind/quality Checks: data validation rules, assertions, tests, reproducibility checks kind/orchestration Pipeline execution: step order, dependencies, caching, parallelization

items.title: Other namespaces
items.text:
Namespace Use it for Examples writer/ Who drafted the record writer/agent, writer/analyst confidence/ How settled the choice or its supporting evidence is confidence/low, confidence/medium, confidence/high topic/ A free-form subject that cuts across kinds topic/missingness, topic/winsorization, topic/multiple-testing plan/ The plan a decision implements or deviates from plan/sap-2026, plan/pap-main axis/<axis>/<value> A choice along a robustness or specification axis axis/sample/complete-case, axis/model/ols multiverse/<axis>/<value> The same idea, for projects that call their axes a multiverse multiverse/sample/complete-case, multiverse/se-type/cluster-robust robustness/ The specific robustness check a record covers robustness/placebo, robustness/leave-one-out people/decider/ Person responsible for the choice people/decider/alice people/approver/ Person who reviewed and approved it people/approver/bob people/reviewer/ Optional project convention for a reviewer people/reviewer/carol rejected/ Why a candidate was closed; rejected records only rejected/duplicate, rejected/merged, rejected/withdrawn, rejected/no-longer-relevant

Pick one of axis/ and multiverse/ per project.

items.title: Inspect and validate
items.text:
dadrock tags list
dadrock validate tags

The specification also describes #dadr/ annotations in code comments. DADRock does not currently scan or validate those source annotations; that is roadmap work.

items.title: Optional code annotations
items.text:
These conventions describe future tooling; DADRock does not yet scan source comments.

In source-code comments, prefix tags with #dadr/. The same namespaces apply:

Pattern Meaning #dadr/<short-id> Link the surrounding code to a record, e.g. #dadr/01938c20a3b4. A full UUID also works. #dadr/kind/<value> The kind of decision the code implements. #dadr/topic/<value> Free-form topic. #dadr/plan/<id> The plan item the code implements. #dadr/multiverse/<axis>/<value> The value of a robustness or specification axis implemented here. #dadr/confidence/<low\|medium\|high> Author confidence in the annotation.

Several tags can share one comment:

-- #dadr/kind/sample #dadr/topic/missingness
where treatment is not null

items.title: UUID v7 generator
items.text:
Every DADR record has a UUID v7 in its front-matter id field. Its first 12 hex characters are the record's short id, the form to link it by, as in [[01938b8e4d70]]. The filename is up to you; a short kebab-case slug of the title, such as income-preprocessing.md, is suggested.

You may use this page when you are drafting DADR records by hand and need a fresh identifier.

Generate UUID v7

Full UUIDv7 Copy UUID Short id, for links Copy short id

This generator runs entirely in your browser. It writes the current Unix millisecond timestamp into the UUIDv7 timestamp field and fills the remaining random bits with crypto.getRandomValues().

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Warning

DADRock is under heavy development — pre-alpha release. Expect breaking changes.

DADR is the standard: the decision record format and the project vocabulary.

DADRock is a Rust tool that implements DADR. It previews, creates, edits, and validates decision records, and it can direct local LLM agents through tasks on the decision ledger. Everything it writes is a Markdown file you could have written yourself.

dadrock init
dadrock new "Decision title"
dadrock preview
dadrock accept ID
dadrock validate

Running dadrock without a subcommand prints help. preview starts the local web interface, normally at port 4004.

DADRock is a single binary. The web interface is embedded in it, so a complete build needs Rust and Bun; a CLI-only build needs Rust alone.

items.title: From source
items.text:
Clone the repository and build with Cargo:

git clone https://github.com/vincentarelbundock/dadr.git
cd dadr
DADROCK_REQUIRE_JS_BUILD=1 cargo install --path crates/dadrock --bin dadrock
dadrock --version

The first build downloads dependencies and may take several minutes. DADROCK_REQUIRE_JS_BUILD=1 makes the build fail rather than silently skip the web interface when Bun is missing.

items.title: Without the web interface
items.text:
For servers and continuous integration, build the command line only:

cargo install --path crates/dadrock --bin dadrock --features no-js-build

dadrock preview then shows a notice instead of the interface; every other command works. Install from a pinned revision for reproducibility.

items.title: Optional: a local agent
items.text: Drafting and conflict checks use a local agent speaking the Agent Client Protocol, such as claude-agent-acp. DADRock detects one on PATH automatically; see LLM agents to configure a specific provider. Nothing else in DADRock depends on it.

items.title: Next
items.text: Open the web interface or the standalone app, set up your editor, or read what a Data Analysis Decision Record is.

items.title: Standalone app
items.text: You can also use DADRock through a cross-platform standalone app built with Tauri. It opens a project folder in its own window and shows the same interface as the web interface. Download it for macOS, Windows, or Linux from the latest release. The macOS and Windows downloads include the dadrock command. On Linux the app runs the dadrock it finds on PATH, so install DADRock too; the Linux packages of the app depend on the dadrock package.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Projects

Command Description init Create a Dadrock dadr/ directory. demo Seed a new project with a named DADR example. preview Serve the local web review UI. config Print the resolved project layout. dir Print the discovered Dadrock project directory (dadr/).

Records

Command Description new Create a candidate decision record from the active candidate template. list List records, optionally filtered by lifecycle status, tag, or query. history Show a decision's versions as a graph, newest first, with the reason for each change and each version's text edits from Git. diff Compare two records: title, tags, and body without ## Supersedes. accept Accept a candidate decision, or several together with --with. reject Reject a candidate decision. supersede Link accepted successors to the records they supersede and move those records to the archive. status Inspect one record's lifecycle status or run lifecycle transitions.

Validation

Command Description validate Run project validation, or target records, links, tags, or changes. tags Inspect DADR tag usage.

Agents

Command Description agent Call a configured local ACP agent for candidate drafting. task Discover, inspect, and run Dadrock task packages. mcp Serve Dadrock MCP tools over stdio.

Help

Command Description help Show top-level help or detailed metadata for one command. commands List command metadata for automation and command discovery. completions Generate a shell completion script.

items.title: Editors
items.text: DADR records are plain Markdown files. You can write and edit them in any editor and run dadrock preview alongside it to review, accept, and validate them in the web interface.

items.title: VS Code and Positron
items.text:
The repository contains one extension implementation in editors/vscode. It opens the DADRock web interface inside an editor panel: it starts dadrock preview for the current workspace, shows the local page in a webview, and stops the server when asked. Positron uses the same extension source.

From a repository checkout, build the binary and the extension and install it with the editor's command-line tool:

make vscode      # VS Code
make positron    # Positron
make editors     # both

These targets need the editor CLI, Rust, Bun, and Node. The extension they build bundles the dadrock binary. Reload the editor window afterwards to pick up the new extension.

items.title: Commands
items.text: Command Description Dadrock: Start Start the preview server for the current workspace. Dadrock: Stop Stop the preview server. Dadrock: Restart Stop and start again. Dadrock: Show Panel Reveal the DADRock panel. Dadrock: Init Run dadrock init in the current workspace.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Setting Default Description dadrock.binaryPath "" Absolute path to the dadrock binary. Empty means the bundled binary, then dadrock on PATH. dadrock.autoStart false Start DADRock automatically when a workspace containing dadr/inbox, dadr/ledger, or dadr/archive opens.

The extension is not published on the Visual Studio Marketplace or Open VSX. GitHub releases attach its VSIX files: one per platform with the dadrock binary bundled (macOS arm64 and x64, Linux x64, Windows x64), and a universal one that needs dadrock on PATH or dadrock.binaryPath. Install one with the editor's --install-extension option. There are no separate official extensions for Cursor, RStudio, or Neovim.

items.title: Web interface
items.text:
After installing DADRock, start the web interface from your analysis project with:

dadrock preview

Then open the address it prints, normally http://127.0.0.1:4004, in your browser. dadrock preview DIRECTORY serves another project, and --port picks another port.
